title: Hatchet Game will soar to new heights on September 5 | Jackson Star and Herald - Ripley and Ravenswood | wvnews.com
text:
RIPLEY, W.Va. (WV News) -- The Hatchet Game is one of the most anticipated sporting events in Jackson County.
This year, the football game is the second of the season, and both Ripley and Ravenswood High Schools are gearing up for a high-energy, stadium-packed game.
However, not all of the excitement will happen on the field on September 5 at Ripley High's Memorial Stadium.
One of the most stirring events will take place in the air around 7:05 p.m. as a Ripley High School student will complete a flyover of the stadium.
Rihya Bennett will be taking the controls in a Cessna airplane with her flight leader, Chuck Heilmann. They will be followed in a plane flown by a student from Mason County with pilot Joey Rivera, who is both that student and Rihya’s instructor.
They will "hold" at Walmart, go around Cedar Lakes, and fly from the north end zone to the south. There will be narration to inform the crowd about what is happening, with Rihya calling in the flight.
“We may even have a little surprise in store,” Rivera said.
Rihya, a 16-year-old junior, has been flying with the Young Eagles through the Experimental Aircraft Association (EAA) for about two years. She became involved with them after attending her first General Chuck Yeager Aviation Day, also known as YeagerFest, in 2023 at the Jackson County Airport.
YeagerFest, now in its third year, celebrates the legacy of General Chuck Yeager and his contributions to flight. A major draw to the event is the free Young Eagle flights offered by the EAA. This year’s YeagerFest is Saturday, September 27, from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.
“I had begged mom and dad to let us fly to the beach instead of a long car ride,” Rihya recalled. “I got turned down, but I was determined to find a way to get into a plane.”
Her father, Roy, had worked with Chuck Heilmann, a longtime member of the local EAA Chapter 1336.
“Chuck actually took me up before YeagerFest,” Rihya said. “He flew us over my house and over to Ravenswood. The sunset was so beautiful with all the colors. I didn’t know what to think; I was so stunned.”
Heilmann told her about YeagerFest and the Young Eagles. Before that happened, Rihya had to undergo foot surgery.
“I was at home, not getting to go to school, with no socialization,” she recalled. “I needed social interaction so badly, so I begged to go. Dad lifted me into the plane, where Chuck was my pilot.”
That was it for Rihya. She knew that aviation would be a part of her life.
Rivera described it as, “When you get the aviation bug, you’re toast.”
To pursue ground school and flight lessons is a commitment of time and money.
“I have serious conversations with the students and their parents,” Rivera, a licensed instructor, said. “With Rihya, I could see in her eyes and that ‘perma-grin’ she had.”
Rihya is currently in ground school, where she is learning the fundamentals, such as weather-related information and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulations. There are tests along the way. Ground school is 60 hours, and earning a flight certificate takes a minimum of 40 hours.
“I’m at the airport two days a week for about one to one and a half hours,” Rihya said. “I have to balance it with my other activities and schoolwork.”
To be able to complete this flyover at arguably her school’s most important game is something Rihya is looking forward to – but not just for the thrill.
“This can show the student body that they can do the same thing,” she said.
Promoting aviation as a career, while demonstrating that Jackson County Airport has the facility and the instructor on hand, means the most to Rivera.
“We want to open people’s eyes to the possibilities that they have right in their own backyard,” he said. “There are so many aviation-related careers, such as mechanics, engineers, designers, dispatchers, service providers, and, of course, pilots.”
While Rihya doesn’t intend for aviation to be her primary career, she does plan to become a private pilot.
“The one thing I want to say is thank you to my parents,” she said. “They have supported me in anything I’ve ever done. This flyover is something they’re very proud of me for doing, and in some ways, it’s promoting women in aviation.”
Eyes on an aviation career
While he will not be part of the flyover, another Ripley High School student has chosen his life path.
Brody Horn, 16, has begun training that he plans to lead him to a career as a commercial pilot eventually.
Like Rihya, Brody got his start by coming to a Young Eagles event at Jackson County Airport on May 4, 2025.
“My great-grandpa, Bill Weekley, loves aviation, and he used to fly,” Brody said. “He kept encouraging me to go see what it was all about.”
When the Young Eagles opportunity came to try a flight for free, Brody said he thought it might be fun. He found out he was wrong.
“It was more than fun,” he said. “The best way I can describe it is I felt alive. I don’t know any other words.”
On May 10, he began his instruction with Rivera. His "flight path" differs from Rihya’s because his goal is not the same, with a focus on commercial flight.
“I am prepping for a solo flight,” he said. “That takes a lot of study and practice.”
Rivera said that his student is working on studying emergency procedures with mock tests.
“I have to learn how to fly without instruments,” Brody said. “It’s intimidating.”
He hopes to be ready in about seven months for that solo flight.
In the meantime, he’s had some flight excitement under the direction and guidance of his instructor.
“The first time I landed a plane was one of the best experiences,” Brody said. “It was a pretty nice landing. I’m actually surprised by how well everything has gone so far.”
There is also one other perk for Brody.
“I’ve gotten to have some good conversations with my grandpa,” he said.
